title: Learning clarinet beside Rappolo, and hearing Chicago jazz
summary: Mares learned clarinet sitting next to Rappolo, who never played a solo the same way; he heard Oliver, the Dodds and others in Chicago.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah, she's a year under me. And Vic, getting back to Vic, I thought Vic would have been a real fine tenor man, but he just left it fall on the wayside. I took up clarinet and learned it from rap. I sat next to rap for a year, but I never could learn rap style because, for instance, I used to ask rap, how did you make this lick? How did you make this break? And he used to call me Oibs. And he used to say, well, Oibs, I really can't tell you. I'll make them when I get to them, which was true with rap. Rap never played the same solo back, or he never played the same thing. It was right from the heart, right on the spot.
You can tell that from the Tin Roof Blues. There's three masters. That's right.

They were all different because rap couldn't play the same solos. We have Raymond Boyk in that same category. I could be rehearsing here and tell Raymond would come out with a good solo, and I said, that's the one I want, Raymond. Well, I can't get it back because Raymond's not going to play it anymore the same way. Well, those fellas are really playing from the heart, Bill. Then we came along, and I started out. I went up to Spring Hill College, and that was around the 25, 26. But before that, I had a chance to go to Chicago, and I heard King Oliver and all the greats. Of course, at that time, I didn't appreciate it. I didn't know exactly how great they were until now, you see. And it didn't mean that much to me at that particular time, but I was hearing Baby Dodds and Johnny Dodds and Lee Collins and all the greats, King Oliver and all the Austin High boys and Bix and so forth and all that, but I didn't appreciate it, like I say, because I didn't know what it was all about at the time. That's right. And I would have given my right arm to play clarinet, but for some reason, I just didn't get to be good with it. So Paul told me, look, boy, you either got to be good or it's no good. So I dropped out of it. And, of course, I never lost interest in jazz. I always had it in my heart, and I always went along with it. Wait, I'll catch you somebody else.
